commenti.body: Which film director is a 21st-century Alfred Hitchcock?

Crash 2004. I’m still confused by the hate it gets. I saw it this week. People kept saying it never should won the Oscar. But their reason was that it’s about people who orgasm to car crashes. No it’s not. The main theme I took away from it was that anyone can be racist, and that Ludacris couldn’t act his way out of a paper bag. I think it won because it made the most powerful statement out of all of the films nominated in that category. I never want to see it again, but watching it for the first time in 2024… so any race can be racist. Did people think that was the message 20 years ago?

What are some romantic examples of the "Person Discovers a Family Secret" genre? It doesn't have to be some big thing (in fact the smaller the better) but basically a partner discovering something about their partner (past or current secret or thoughts) that makes them look at their partner differently etc.
The first name that came up in my mind is Jordan Peele!

45 Years

Secrets and Lies

Incendies

History of Violence

Watched Paris Texas yesterday. I can appreciate the beautiful cinematography and the plot and emotional themes were interesting enough but how do people get past that Travis is an abusive alcoholic pedophile who kidnaps his son who he previously deserted? I cannot feel an ounce of sympathy and the fact that he’s framed like some tortured soul on a redemptive journey is ridiculous to me. This movie is pretty acclaimed so I was just wondering how people feel about it about it.
*L'Heure d'été* (*Summer Hours*)
Seems more familial than romantic from the description but good shout nonetheless; had never heard about it and I need to check out more Assayas.

All in the watch-list, funnily enough (though from what I can tell only 45 Years fits the bill, as Secrets and Lies & Incendies seem familial rather than romantic, and History of Violence about an action rather than secret).

It's been years since I've watched it and I liked it a lot from what I remember but the truth is that it's a reveal that works only because of narrative "trickery", namely because of how late it comes in the film, by the time when the audience has already accepted and are deeply invested into a seemingly innocent Travis. (If it had, say, revealed Travis' actions early, his past would hang as a black cloud over the entire film and likely make any sort of redemption impossible in the audience's eyes. Though this does not mean that one approach is more honest/correct than the other.) Even with that, plenty of people have a hard time swallowing this pseudo-redemptive arch (there was a recent post here with similar "complaints" as yours that seem to have been deleted).
I do remember feeling similar in the way that it is revealed towards the end of the film so you are already invested
Another obvious example is *Chinatown*, if you haven't seen it. Jack Nicholson's Jake Gittes discovers a very disturbing secret about Faye Dunaway's Evelyn Cross-Mulwray.
I'm not sure there is one, any more than there was a 19th century Hitchcock.

I was 16 when I first watched it and remember it leaving me deeply moved. Cried at two separate scenes. Ended up randomly watching it again at 31 with my gf (a few months ago) and felt like it was hitting me over the head with it's righteous message. It's also a movie that really plays on your emotions rather than causes you to be reflective or allows you to appreciate it on a filmaking level. 


Sure any group of people can be racist, if it takes this movie telling you that than you haven't had many experiences in life. If anything the musical composition should be recognized as that's what did most of the heavy lifting. I had the same experience with American Beauty on the 2nd watch.


If you wanna see a better version of the "entangled strangers" style of movie Short Cuts by Robert Altman would be worth watching in my opinion.

I actually didn’t mind seeing it for the first time in 2024. We were inundated with CRT a decade ago. But learning about racism in Asia made me realize new things. Are we allowed to discuss this?

I didn’t mind Crash because I don’t feel that it pandered, like Get Out. Crash was like a tableau, a day in the life. Crash doesn’t insult, and I cared about the characters. The irony of the scene where Matt Dillon rescues Thandie Newton from the wrecked car is… he sexually assaulted her previously in the film… it’s such a scene. Your assaulter saves your life. Crash is disturbing and haunting. It certainly causes thoughts!

I had a question about Come and See that probably isn't worth a whole thread. Is "Flyora" a common name in Belarus? I like learning about names and I saw that it means "flower" but from what I can tell that's not really an actual name most people, let alone boys, have in Russia/Belarus. How does that change how we should look at Flyora? Does it bring him to a more allegorical level?

I have seen (and it’s obviously great) but if we start bringing in Noirs then every film in that ”genre” starring a femme fatale (not an apt categorisation for Dunaway’s character, but still) might as well be included. (Though in the case of Chinatown the secret is about something done *unto* the Dunaway character, whereas I was thinking about something that a character/the partner has done.)
hey everyone! i'm celebrating my 21st birthday in the city by watching a film with my brother -- should i see seven samurai (1954) or nostalgia (1983)?
hollis frampton's nostalgia might be a fun birthday watch, tarkovsky's seems a bit somber for all that.

Saw *Fallen Leaves* last night. It was my first Kaurismaki. I was instantly won over by the poignant social commentry (all the meat at the beginning and the "You'll go far" scene are, for example, so short and memorable), empathetic portrayal of working class characters that doesn't descend into corny sentimentality, deadpan humor, subtle acting and toying with romcom conventions. I'll definitely dive into his filmography.
He would be my pick too. If I'm not mistaken, he has just the right amount of both critical acclaim and popularity.

People are aware it's just a story and not real. The story teller asks them to extend empathy, understanding, and forgiveness to Travis, and they go with it so the story can happen. People understand the importance of story telling and want to participate in it. People understand that storytelling is an activity that works best when they suspend their judgement for a while and allow the story teller to show them things. They understand that they don't know everything and that story telling is an opportunity to learn. They put their judgement, their righteousness and their egos aside for a while because they understand this is the only way they can learn anything of value.
Check out *Man Without a Past* and *Ariel*, the first one is his best film.
Thank you for the recommendation.
